title: Bessel Observatory
description: One numerical observatory, expressed independently and idiomatically in 31 programming languages. Read x values, approximate the Bessel function J0 in separate OS processes, and export ordered CSV observations.
goals: Make language differences visible through equivalent observable behavior.
Exercise file and console I/O, interactive input, command-line arguments, graceful error handling, actual OS multiprocessing, and special-function mathematics.
Keep each numerical kernel in its language; Bash explicitly uses its conventional awk floating-point utility. Low-level adapters provide missing OS services, never a shared Bessel implementation.
Make setup requirements and validation evidence explicit.
Compare pointers, references, byte/element offsets and string manipulation honestly across memory models.
methodology: Specify a shared input/output and failure contract before writing implementations.
Use midpoint quadrature of the same integral with 16384 samples in every version.
Choose native idioms and standard libraries; use a named dialect or OS extension when a language lacks process APIs.
Use bounded process batches, or native process pools, preserving input order.
Validate numerical answers against independent high-precision reference values, not just against another translation.
Check invalid input, stdin, worker limits, file failures, empty input and argument misuse. Record unavailable toolchains as untested.
Document SQL input/argument adaptations, process startup overhead, and floating-point differences.
Keep unsafe memory demonstrations isolated; preserve allocation lifetime and bounds, then rerun the behavioral checks. Display an explicit memory/string feature map for every language.
Use functional comments and purpose/input/output/caller contracts; use native block comments where available, # comments for Python, and ERA blocks for Perligata.

contract.workers: Integer from 1 through 16; maximum simultaneous numeric worker processes, not total lifetime process count.
contract.input: UTF-8/ASCII text, one decimal real per line; leading/trailing whitespace ignored; lines beginning # are comments. First blank line or EOF finishes in both file and interactive modes.
contract.domain: Finite real x in [-1000,1000]; at most 4096 accepted values.
contract.errors: Invalid value lines produce diagnostics on stderr and are skipped. No valid values, excess values, bad arguments, I/O failures or worker failures terminate nonzero. Ordinary exceptions become readable diagnostics.
contract.output: CSV columns x,j0,worker_pid; one row per accepted value in original order. Output is written after all calculations succeed, and replaces an existing target. OS PIDs and numeric formatting vary.
contract.help: --help prints usage. Hidden --worker modes, where present, are implementation details.
contract.portability: Linux/POSIX is the comparison baseline. Ada/Fortran bindings assume LP64; BASIC/COBOL target Linux x86-64. Some process-launch implementations also work on macOS/Windows. Native numeric parsers may accept additional literal spellings; the common format is ordinary decimal or e-notation. RPG uses IBM i CALL parameters, DSPLY and IFS paths; its separate integration contract is rpg_setup.txt. Oberon bounds line length to 4095 bytes. PostScript requires 64-bit Ghostscript on Linux with process/file access and bounds input lines to 4096 bytes.

mathematics.function: Bessel function of the first kind, order zero: J0(x)
mathematics.motivation: An oscillating radial wave profile; Bessel functions arise in circular vibration and wave problems.
mathematics.caveats: This is a finite quadrature demonstration, not a certified special-function library. Domain and sample count are fixed to keep comparisons well resolved. Reduction order, compensated summation and sinpi cause tiny differences; no bitwise equivalence or speed ranking is claimed.

sql_adapter.arguments: psql -X -d observatory -v values=0,1,5 -v workers=2 -v output=results.csv -f bessel.sql
sql_adapter.interactive: Omit values and input to receive a psql prompt for a comma-separated list.
sql_adapter.file_input: -v input=/absolute/server/path/values.txt; pg_read_file reads on the database server and needs its file-read privileges. Output is local to the psql client.
sql_adapter.setup: Use a dedicated database with dblink installed or extension creation privileges. Connections must authenticate to the same database; optional -v conn=... uses a libpq connection string or service. Do not pass -1/--single-transaction: new backend connections must see the committed extension.
sql_adapter.state: Creates dblink if absent and session-local temporary tables; workers execute SQL aggregates without shared functions. Backend PID is the worker_pid.

limitations: This is a language study, not a process-startup benchmark: some versions reuse workers, others launch one child per value.
Runtime startup often costs more than the calculation; large JVM/BEAM runs are intentionally not optimized for throughput.
Error cleanup covers ordinary I/O and worker failures; signal handling is runtime-dependent. The examples do not promise transactional output under disk-full failures or process termination.
GNU Smalltalk must be launched from the project directory because its workers use the relative bessel.st path.
SQL requires a running PostgreSQL server; it cannot be executed as a standalone portable SQL file in SQLite/MySQL.
Use the supplied BASIC build helper: FreeBASIC generates a C intermediate, so compiling the same basename in the source directory can collide with the C edition.
Bash orchestrates the embedded awk numerical kernel because Bash arithmetic is integer-only.
Oberon-2 uses the supplied C adapter for checked OS and stdio interfaces; its quadrature and raw-address traversal are Oberon.

Perligata uses BesselPerligata.pm for regex validation, unchanged line reads, temporary storage and checked POSIX/exception services. Native perlege converts Roman numerals, so it cannot preserve this input contract. Opening/writing/closing files, quadrature and scheduling remain in Latin.
RPG requires IBM i setup described in rpg_setup.txt; failed or timed-out runs retain work rows, and submitted jobs may finish after parent failure.
Raw pointer arithmetic is unavailable in several listed languages; their native reference/offset models are documented instead.
PostScript retains the 1e-10 tolerance using software fixed-point arithmetic entirely in PostScript; Ghostscript native real arithmetic is too imprecise. It requires a 64-bit integer build.

PostScript requires Linux /proc and Ghostscript %pipe% access. Its POSIX shell only execs another interpreter; there is no foreign-language helper. Restricted printer-oriented OS profiles may block execution even with -dNOSAFER. Run from the project directory, or supply -sBesselSource before --.

validation.status: See per-language report; source review is not a substitute for compilation/execution.
validation.source_browser: 31 offline highlighted program pages, plus highlighted support code; embedded raw text and hashes match the source files.

sources.title: Oxford Oberon-2 compiler and library sources
IBM i IFS UTF-8 file services
Ghostscript language limits and file extensions

languages.name: Pascal
languages.idioms: Procedures, dynamic arrays, try/except and try/finally, TProcess ownership.
languages.multiprocessing: TProcess child executables in bounded batches
languages.memory: PDouble dereference and Inc(Cursor) traverse a live Double array in element-sized steps.
languages.strings: Trim, comment-prefix detection, numeric conversion, string concatenation, CSV formatting.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers and graceful errors
adaptations.constraint: This edition targets Free Pascal’s Object Pascal libraries rather than minimal standard Pascal.
adaptations.approach: TProcess launches separate copies of the executable with pipes. Native try/except reports failures, and try/finally terminates/reaps children and frees objects.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Free Pascal with SysUtils and Process. Exception support is native to the chosen dialect, not an emulated feature.

languages.name: Ada
languages.idioms: Strong types, range checks, generic Float_IO, exception handlers, explicit C imports.
languages.multiprocessing: POSIX fork, pipe and waitpid
languages.memory: Borrowed in-out scalar reference, System.Address and Storage_Offset byte arithmetic in complete pipe transfers.
languages.strings: Trim, string slices, argument strings, image conversion and diagnostic concatenation.

adaptations.constraint: Ada tasks do not by themselves provide the separate OS processes required here.
adaptations.approach: Import POSIX fork, pipe, read/write and waitpid through Interfaces.C; Batch runs the Ada kernel in each child.
adaptations.tradeoff: The C ABI declarations assume a POSIX LP64 system; tasking alone cannot replace this process boundary.

adaptations.constraint: Ada already has exceptions; imported C functions still return status codes.
adaptations.approach: Check transfer and child statuses explicitly, raise descriptive exceptions, and catch invalid numbers locally so reading continues.
adaptations.tradeoff: The foreign-call boundary needs explicit checks even though the surrounding control flow uses native exception handling.

languages.name: BASIC
languages.idioms: Structured BASIC, typed arrays, line input and explicit return-code checks.
languages.multiprocessing: POSIX fork and binary pipes via C ABI
languages.memory: ByRef parameters, Double Ptr, dereference and cursor += 1 across a locally owned numeric array.
languages.strings: Trim, Left, StrPtr, C-string end-pointer validation and CSV concatenation.

adaptations.constraint: This FreeBASIC edition needs POSIX process and pipe services through its foreign-function interface.
adaptations.approach: Extern C declarations bind fork, pipe, read/write and waitpid. The child computes J0 with BASIC Double arithmetic.
adaptations.tradeoff: Targets Linux x86-64 and its ABI. Use the supplied build helper to keep generated C intermediates away from bessel.c.

adaptations.constraint: This edition uses explicit success/failure results at parsing, file and OS boundaries.
adaptations.approach: Number returns Boolean acceptance; invalid values are skipped. Fatal checks call Fail to print a diagnostic and End 1.
adaptations.tradeoff: There is no automatic exception unwinding in this implementation; the checked control paths own resource handling.

languages.name: COBOL
languages.idioms: Divisions, paragraphs, PICTURE fields, EVALUATE, file status and ON SIZE ERROR.
languages.multiprocessing: CBL_GC_FORK with POSIX pipes and waitpid
languages.memory: USAGE POINTER, ADDRESS OF, a LINKAGE reference, and SET pointer UP BY LENGTH OF current-sample.
languages.strings: FUNCTION TRIM, reference modification, TEST-NUMVAL-F, STRING and edited PICTURE output.

adaptations.constraint: This GnuCOBOL edition uses operation-specific status handling rather than a general try/catch block.
adaptations.approach: FILE STATUS and check-file detect I/O errors; TEST-NUMVAL-F and ON SIZE ERROR reject malformed or overflowing input. Fatal paths STOP RUN RETURNING 1.
adaptations.tradeoff: File, numeric and worker statuses must each be checked explicitly.

adaptations.constraint: Process creation is supplied by the selected GnuCOBOL runtime and POSIX services.
adaptations.approach: CBL_GC_FORK creates children; binary POSIX pipes carry the COBOL-computed results and waitpid verifies completion.
adaptations.tradeoff: The foreign calls and numeric layouts target GnuCOBOL on Linux x86-64, not arbitrary COBOL runtimes.

languages.name: Fortran
languages.idioms: Modules, numeric kinds, typed array pointers, IEEE checks, IOSTAT and ISO_C_BINDING.
languages.multiprocessing: POSIX fork and pipes through ISO_C_BINDING
languages.memory: C_LOC / C_F_POINTER produce typed array pointers; pointer sections shift the view using array descriptors. Raw address addition is not portable standard Fortran.
languages.strings: TRIM, ADJUSTL, VERIFY, character slices, concatenation, internal numeric READ and formatted WRITE.

adaptations.constraint: This edition needs fork/pipe services outside the Fortran language interface.
adaptations.approach: ISO_C_BINDING declarations expose POSIX calls with C-compatible kinds. Each child evaluates the Fortran kernel and sends its result back.
adaptations.tradeoff: Assumes POSIX LP64 and compatible C double storage; it is not a portable coarray implementation.

adaptations.constraint: Fortran I/O exposes IOSTAT/IOMSG rather than structured catchable exceptions.
adaptations.approach: Check numeric READ, file operations, transfers and worker statuses. fail prints to error_unit and calls the bound _exit with status 1.
adaptations.tradeoff: Explicit checks provide readable failures; _exit avoids a compiler-specific ERROR STOP backtrace and uses the POSIX binding.

adaptations.constraint: Portable Fortran does not provide raw C-style address addition.
adaptations.approach: C_LOC/C_F_POINTER expose the owned sample array as a typed pointer; tail points at successive two-element array sections.
adaptations.tradeoff: Offsets are array-descriptor views, not fabricated addresses. The target allocation remains alive throughout the reduction.

languages.name: C
languages.idioms: Structs, explicit ownership, checked return codes, complete pipe transfers.
languages.multiprocessing: POSIX fork, pipe and waitpid
languages.memory: Pointer parameters, array offsets, address-of, dereferences and byte-pointer advancement in checked IPC transfers.
languages.strings: strtod with end-pointer checking, whitespace scanning, strcmp, getline and formatted CSV.

adaptations.constraint: C has no built-in throw/catch exception mechanism.
adaptations.approach: parse, transfer and batch return success flags. Callers inspect errno and child exit status, print diagnostics, and explicitly close/reap resources before returning failure.
adaptations.tradeoff: Error propagation and cleanup must be written at each call boundary; no automatic stack unwinding is supplied.

adaptations.constraint: A POSIX pipe read or write can transfer fewer bytes than requested or be interrupted.
adaptations.approach: transfer advances a byte pointer until the whole payload moves, retries EINTR, and reports EOF or other errors.
adaptations.tradeoff: The binary payload is suitable for forked copies of this executable, not a portable network wire format.

languages.name: Objective-C
languages.idioms: Objective-C class messages, Foundation collections, NSTask, NSError and @try/@finally.
languages.multiprocessing: NSTask child executables
languages.memory: Objective-C object references coexist with C double pointers, one-past array bounds and ++cursor element arithmetic.
languages.strings: NSString trimming/prefix checks, NSScanner parsing, UTF-8 conversion and string formatting.

adaptations.constraint: Foundation and C calls report failures through a mixture of NSError, return values and exceptions.
adaptations.approach: Check C I/O and Foundation write results, translate failures through Fail into NSException, and use @finally for file/buffer and child cleanup.
adaptations.tradeoff: Exceptions are already supported. This edition chooses a common reporting boundary but must still check nonthrowing APIs explicitly.

adaptations.constraint: This edition uses Foundation’s process facilities in addition to the Objective-C language.
adaptations.approach: NSTask relaunches the executable with --worker; NSPipe carries the row, and the parent checks terminationStatus before accepting it.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires macOS Foundation or GNUstep and an Objective-C runtime; the build commands differ by platform.

languages.name: Smalltalk
languages.idioms: Message sends, blocks, inject:into:, OrderedCollection, on:do: and ensure:.
languages.multiprocessing: External GNU Smalltalk VMs via FileStream popen:
languages.memory: Object references and indexed collection access. This edition does not expose raw pointers or pretend block fork creates OS processes.
languages.strings: trimSeparators, stream-based parsing, character tests, copyReplaceAll: and comma-delimited output.

adaptations.constraint: Smalltalk block fork is a language-level process, not the separate OS worker required here.
adaptations.approach: FileStream popen: starts external GNU Smalltalk VMs, and a getpid C binding reports their OS identity. ensure: closes the process pipes.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires GNU Smalltalk/POSIX and launch from the project directory because bessel.st is a relative worker path. Execution remains untested.

adaptations.constraint: GNU Smalltalk FloatD printing uses a d exponent marker instead of the shared e notation.
adaptations.approach: decimal: replaces d with e when serializing values for CSV and worker arguments.
adaptations.tradeoff: This adapts textual representation only; calculations still use FloatD. Runtime behavior awaits validation.

languages.name: C++
languages.idioms: RAII, unique_ptr, structured bindings, standard exceptions and std::numbers.
languages.multiprocessing: RAII-managed POSIX fork workers
languages.memory: C++ references, unique_ptr ownership, raw pointer parameters/advancement and structured-binding references.
languages.strings: std::string searches, substring position validation, stoi/stod and stream formatting.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers with exception cleanup
adaptations.constraint: The C++20 standard library has no subprocess-launch API; threads would share the parent OS process.
adaptations.approach: Worker wraps POSIX fork and pipes. unique_ptr ownership and the Worker destructor close descriptors and reap children during normal exit or exception unwinding.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires POSIX. Exceptions and RAII are native C++ features; the OS binding is the portability dependency.

languages.name: Rust
languages.idioms: Result and ?, exhaustive match, iterators, ownership and Drop cleanup.
languages.multiprocessing: std::process::Command child executables
languages.memory: Borrowed &[f64] and as_ptr().add(i) dereferences in one documented, bounded unsafe helper.
languages.strings: trim, starts_with, parse, String accumulation and UTF-8 validation.

adaptations.constraint: Rust represents ordinary recoverable failures with Result rather than throw/catch exceptions.
adaptations.approach: Use Result and ? to propagate errors, match to skip invalid lines, and main to emit a diagnostic/status 1. A Worker Drop implementation cleans up children it still owns.
adaptations.tradeoff: Errors remain explicit in signatures. The cleanup wrapper is needed because merely dropping a child-process handle does not reap it.

adaptations.constraint: Dereferencing raw pointers is outside Rust’s safe subset.
adaptations.approach: sum_buffer borrows an immutable slice and contains the educational as_ptr().add(i) dereference in one documented unsafe block.
adaptations.tradeoff: The caller retains live storage; each offset is bounded by the slice. Ordinary Rust would use safe iterator summation.

languages.name: Java
languages.idioms: Records, streams, try-with-resources and ProcessBuilder.
languages.multiprocessing: Separate JVM worker processes
languages.memory: Object references and a ByteBuffer with checked byte-offset reads. Java does not expose raw pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: strip, startsWith, numeric parsing, StringBuilder and Locale.ROOT CSV formatting.

adaptations.constraint: Java does not expose C-style raw pointer arithmetic.
adaptations.approach: observe stores samples in a ByteBuffer and reads them at checked k * Double.BYTES offsets through a shared object reference.
adaptations.tradeoff: Demonstrates byte offsets within managed storage, not addresses. The buffer is an educational alternative to a simple double array.

adaptations.constraint: Java threads alone would not provide independent worker OS PIDs.
adaptations.approach: ProcessBuilder starts a separate JVM in --worker mode with the current classpath. finally terminates and waits for outstanding children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Standard APIs suffice; a JVM starts for each observation, so startup can dominate the calculation.

languages.name: Ruby
languages.idioms: Blocks, Enumerable sum and each_slice, rescue/ensure, CSV library.
languages.multiprocessing: fork with IO.pipe
languages.memory: Object references plus Fiddle::Pointer over a retained packed string; pointer + byte offset and native-double reads.
languages.strings: strip, start_with?, pack/unpack, interpolation, numeric conversion and CSV serialization.

adaptations.constraint: Ordinary Ruby arrays and object references do not provide raw pointer arithmetic.
adaptations.approach: Pack samples into a retained native-double string and use Fiddle::Pointer plus byte offsets to read each value.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires the Fiddle standard library. The packed storage must stay alive and unchanged; normal Ruby would simply sum the array.

adaptations.constraint: This edition relies on POSIX fork support.
adaptations.approach: fork and IO.pipe create numeric children; Process.wait2 checks status. rescue handles errors and ensure closes pipes and reaps outstanding children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires a fork-capable platform. Exceptions and ensure are native Ruby, so no exception emulation is needed.

languages.name: JavaScript
languages.idioms: ES modules, async iteration, promises, Promise.all, try/finally.
languages.multiprocessing: child_process.fork with IPC messages, not worker threads
languages.memory: ArrayBuffer/DataView references and checked byte-offset arithmetic. These are not raw addresses.
languages.strings: trim, startsWith, regex validation, template strings and array joining.

adaptations.constraint: The browser JavaScript execution model does not provide the required command-line OS workers.
adaptations.approach: Target Node.js and use child_process.fork with IPC. worker resolves its Promise only after receiving a result and a successful child close event.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Node.js, not a browser. Promise.all coordinates ordering; child processes perform the numerical work.

adaptations.constraint: JavaScript references do not expose raw memory addresses.
adaptations.approach: An ArrayBuffer owns sample storage; DataView reads and writes Float64 values at explicit checked byte offsets.
adaptations.tradeoff: Shows shared-buffer views and offsets, with no raw-pointer arithmetic or foreign helper.

languages.name: Python
languages.idioms: Structural match/case, type hints, generators, context managers, argparse, fsum. A small ctypes example demonstrates pointer offsets.
languages.multiprocessing: ProcessPoolExecutor with spawn context
languages.memory: ctypes array ownership, byref(array, byte_offset), POINTER(c_double) casts and contents dereference. math.fsum remains the reducer.
languages.strings: strip, startswith, float parsing, f-strings and csv.writer serialization.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers with safe startup
adaptations.constraint: Spawned Python processes import the module, so an unguarded CLI would start recursively.
adaptations.approach: ProcessPoolExecutor uses an explicit spawn context and ordered map. The __main__ guard separates importable worker definitions from the command-line entry point.
adaptations.tradeoff: Standard-library facilities suffice. Spawn incurs interpreter/import overhead and requires an importable worker function.

adaptations.constraint: Ordinary Python objects provide references, not C-style pointer arithmetic.
adaptations.approach: A ctypes double array owns the samples. byref supplies byte offsets, cast provides typed pointers, and contents reads them while the array stays alive.
adaptations.tradeoff: This is an explicit ctypes example with manual bounds/lifetime reasoning; math.fsum remains the numerical reducer.

languages.name: Lua
languages.idioms: Tables, closures, protected calls, to-be-closed local, small explicit modules.
languages.multiprocessing: luaposix fork, pipes and wait
languages.memory: Tables are passed by reference and process pipes are handles. Standard Lua 5.4 has no raw-pointer arithmetic; no LuaJIT FFI is assumed.
languages.strings: Lua patterns trim whitespace, sub inspects prefixes, string.format and table.concat construct CSV.

adaptations.constraint: Lua’s standard library does not provide the fork/pipe/wait interfaces used here.
adaptations.approach: Load luaposix modules for process creation, pipe transfers, child PIDs and wait status; keep the numerical kernel in Lua.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Lua 5.4 plus luaposix on POSIX. Missing-module errors are caught by the protected entry call.

adaptations.constraint: Lua provides protected calls rather than try/catch syntax.
adaptations.approach: pcall catches numeric, batch and top-level errors. Batch cleanup closes descriptors and waits before rethrowing; a to-be-closed local scopes the output file.
adaptations.tradeoff: Protected calls are native error handling. Child-resource cleanup is explicit, and the output scope requires Lua 5.4.

languages.name: Julia
languages.idioms: Multiple dispatch, generators, named tuples, do-blocks, sinpi, pmap.
languages.multiprocessing: Distributed.addprocs / pmap on OS workers
languages.memory: Ptr byte arithmetic and unsafe_load within GC.@preserve; the owning Float64 array stays alive and unmodified.
languages.strings: strip, startswith, parse, interpolation and Printf output.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers with definitions available
adaptations.constraint: Separate Julia processes need the observe definition loaded before they can execute it.
adaptations.approach: Distributed.addprocs creates workers; @everywhere includes the source there. The PROGRAM_FILE guard prevents recursive CLI execution, pmap preserves ordering, and finally removes workers.
adaptations.tradeoff: Uses the Distributed standard library and pays process/loading overhead. This design is source-reviewed; execution remains untested.

adaptations.constraint: A raw Ptr alone does not keep its owning array alive.
adaptations.approach: GC.@preserve retains samples while pointer arithmetic and unsafe_load read aligned Float64 elements.
adaptations.tradeoff: Bounds and lifetime are the programmer’s responsibility in this demonstration; ordinary array iteration avoids these unsafe reads.

languages.name: Perl
languages.idioms: Lexical filehandles, regexes, eval/die, list processing and POSIX module.
languages.multiprocessing: fork with pipe handles
languages.memory: Scalar, array and filehandle references, including referenced child records. This edition uses portable Perl references, not fabricated raw addresses.
languages.strings: Regex trimming, numeric-token recognition, interpolation, printf and string-length checks.

adaptations.constraint: Perl 5.20 already supplies eval/die, but cleanup here is implemented explicitly around eval.
adaptations.approach: batch saves $@ immediately after eval, closes pipe handles and waits for tracked children, then rethrows the original error. The entry boundary prints it and exits nonzero.
adaptations.tradeoff: Cleanup must preserve the original exception; references to child records provide ownership without raw pointers.

languages.name: Swift
languages.idioms: Value types, typed error enum, guard, defer and Foundation Process.
languages.multiprocessing: Foundation Process child executables
languages.memory: Foundation class references plus withUnsafeBufferPointer, advanced(by:) and pointee inside the buffer lifetime.
languages.strings: Trimming, hasPrefix, UTF-8 conversion, splitting lines and interpolation.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers and graceful errors
adaptations.constraint: Swift concurrency tasks alone do not provide independent OS workers.
adaptations.approach: Foundation Process launches this executable in --worker mode. Typed thrown errors reach do/catch, while defer terminates and waits for outstanding children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Foundation Process on the target platform; process startup occurs per observation. No exception emulation is needed; execution remains untested.

adaptations.constraint: An Array’s unsafe buffer pointer is only valid within its borrowing scope.
adaptations.approach: withUnsafeBufferPointer contains every advanced(by:) and pointee read, with offsets bounded by buffer.count.
adaptations.tradeoff: The example relies on manual bounds reasoning but does not let the pointer escape; ordinary reduction could avoid unsafe access.

languages.name: Erlang
languages.idioms: Pattern matching, tail recursion, mailbox receive, ports and try/after.
languages.multiprocessing: Ports start separate escript OS VMs; not just BEAM processes
languages.memory: Immutable values and opaque port handles. BEAM terms do not expose raw memory pointers or pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: string:trim, string:to_float/to_integer, float_to_list and io:format.

adaptations.constraint: Erlang spawn creates a BEAM process, which does not satisfy the separate OS-process requirement.
adaptations.approach: open_port starts another escript VM per observation. Port messages carry output and exit status; each worker reports os:getpid().
adaptations.tradeoff: Starting a VM per value is expensive. Batches bound concurrency and collect imposes a 30-second receive timeout.

adaptations.constraint: BEAM terms do not expose raw addresses or pointer arithmetic.
adaptations.approach: Use immutable lists for values, explicit recursion state for the sum, and opaque port handles for worker resources.
adaptations.tradeoff: This demonstrates Erlang value and handle semantics; it makes no raw-pointer claim.

languages.name: Haskell
languages.idioms: Pure sample generation, Either, pattern matching, scoped foreign memory, explicit IO and bracketed child lifetimes.
languages.multiprocessing: System.Process child executables
languages.memory: withArray brackets a foreign allocation; plusPtr byte offsets and peek occur explicitly in IO. Numeric sample generation remains pure.
languages.strings: Whitespace/prefix pattern matching, readMaybe, string concatenation, show and line streams.

adaptations.constraint: Dereferencing foreign memory is an IO effect, while the sample sequence can remain pure.
adaptations.approach: withArray owns a temporary allocation; plusPtr advances by Double-sized byte offsets and peek reads within that scope.
adaptations.tradeoff: j0 returns IO Double and copies samples into foreign storage for the memory example; the sample-generation function remains pure.

adaptations.constraint: Lazy hGetContents output must be consumed while its pipe is still open.
adaptations.approach: Nested withCreateProcess scopes retain workers; evaluate (length row) forces each result before waiting and leaving its resource scope.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires process and unix packages. Bracketed lifetimes and exceptions are native library facilities, not an emulated exception system.

languages.name: OCaml
languages.idioms: Algebraic variants, pattern matching, recursive list processing, Fun.protect.
languages.multiprocessing: Unix.fork and pipes
languages.memory: ref cells, shared values and mutable array/channel handles. Portable OCaml does not expose raw address arithmetic.
languages.strings: String.trim, prefix indexing, float_of_string, concatenation and Printf.

adaptations.constraint: The selected process interface comes from the Unix library.
adaptations.approach: Unix.fork creates numeric children, pipes carry results, and waitpid is matched against WEXITED 0. Fun.protect closes channels and reaps children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Unix library linkage and POSIX fork support. Exceptions and cleanup combinators are native OCaml facilities.

adaptations.constraint: Portable OCaml does not expose raw pointer arithmetic.
adaptations.approach: A ref cell holds the mutable sum; lists retain input values and referenced child records hold PIDs/channel handles.
adaptations.tradeoff: The comparison uses managed references and handles rather than claiming they are raw addresses.

languages.name: Lisp
languages.idioms: Conditions, a skip-value restart, LOOP, WITH-OPEN-FILE and UNWIND-PROTECT.
languages.multiprocessing: SBCL run-program with asynchronous OS processes
languages.memory: SBCL vector-sap, sap+ byte offsets and sap-ref-double within with-pinned-objects. This is an explicitly implementation-specific pointer example.
languages.strings: STRING-TRIM, READ-FROM-STRING with reader evaluation disabled, SUBSEQ and FORMAT.

adaptations.constraint: These process and memory facilities are implementation-specific in this Common Lisp edition.
adaptations.approach: SBCL run-program starts asynchronous worker interpreters. vector-sap and sap+ traverse the sample vector while with-pinned-objects prevents GC relocation.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires SBCL; the explicit pointer example and OS interfaces are not portable ANSI Common Lisp.

adaptations.constraint: Common Lisp already supplies conditions and restarts, allowing recovery without abandoning the input session.
adaptations.approach: read-values installs a handler that invokes skip-value; restart-case discards the malformed observation. Fatal conditions reach the outer handler-case.
adaptations.tradeoff: No exception workaround is needed. Recovery is deliberately limited to the numeric-input operation.

languages.name: Prolog
languages.idioms: Relations, unification, recursive accumulation, catch/3, setup_call_cleanup/3.
languages.multiprocessing: library(process) creates separate SWI-Prolog OS workers
languages.memory: Logical variables and unification plus stream/process handles; no exposed raw addresses or pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: normalize_space, sub_string, number_string, atom/string conversion and format.

adaptations.constraint: This edition needs SWI-Prolog’s process library in addition to logical evaluation.
adaptations.approach: process_create starts a separate SWI executable per value; nested setup_call_cleanup scopes keep streams and PIDs available until collection or failure.
adaptations.tradeoff: Depends on SWI-Prolog library(process); each observation starts an interpreter. catch and cleanup are supplied facilities.

adaptations.constraint: A predicate may fail logically as well as throw an exception; logical variables are not raw memory pointers.
adaptations.approach: main converts unsuccessful run goals into a program_failed exception and catches it for a diagnostic/status 1. Results travel through unification and stream/worker terms.
adaptations.tradeoff: The interface accounts for both failure modes. Memory examples remain logical bindings and opaque handles.

languages.name: Kotlin
languages.idioms: Data classes, when, collection pipelines, use, require and finally.
languages.multiprocessing: ProcessBuilder starts separate JVMs
languages.memory: JVM object references and ByteBuffer getDouble at checked byte offsets; raw pointers are not available on this target.
languages.strings: trim, startsWith, conversions, string interpolation and Locale.ROOT formatting.

adaptations.constraint: This Kotlin/JVM target has managed references, not Kotlin/Native raw pointers.
adaptations.approach: Use Java ByteBuffer and checked getDouble byte offsets to traverse the shared sample allocation.
adaptations.tradeoff: The memory example describes JVM buffer semantics, not raw address arithmetic.

adaptations.constraint: Threads or coroutines within the JVM would not satisfy the OS-process objective.
adaptations.approach: ProcessBuilder launches BesselKt in separate JVMs using the current classpath. Bounded batches collect rows in order and finally reaps children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Uses JVM interoperability; each observation pays JVM startup cost. use and finally provide native resource/error handling.

languages.name: Go
languages.idioms: Explicit errors, defer, small structs, interfaces and standard-library process APIs.
languages.multiprocessing: os/exec child executables; goroutines only support pipe I/O
languages.memory: A slice owns samples; unsafe.SliceData, unsafe.Add and typed dereference show byte arithmetic, with runtime.KeepAlive.
languages.strings: TrimSpace, HasPrefix, ParseFloat, FormatFloat, bytes.Buffer and formatted CSV.

adaptations.constraint: Go uses explicit error values for ordinary failures; try/catch is not needed for this objective.
adaptations.approach: number, batch and run return errors. Callers propagate them, main prints a diagnostic, and deferred batch cleanup kills and waits for remaining children.
adaptations.tradeoff: Errors must be checked at each call; panic/recover is not used as the normal failure path.

adaptations.constraint: Goroutines execute within the Go runtime and are not separate numerical worker processes.
adaptations.approach: os/exec launches this executable in --worker mode. Child PIDs identify numerical work; internal output-copying goroutines only support pipe I/O.
adaptations.tradeoff: Uses the standard library, with executable startup and buffering overhead for each observation.

languages.name: SQL
languages.idioms: Set-based numeric aggregation, temporary relations, PL/pgSQL exceptions, psql variables.
languages.multiprocessing: dblink_send_query dispatches to separate PostgreSQL backend OS processes
languages.memory: Relational row keys and ordinal offsets are the native analogue. SQL has no raw pointers, object references or pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: btrim, regexp validation, replace, string_to_array, format and array operations.

adaptations.constraint: Portable SQL provides no standalone fork/exec interface for these workers.
adaptations.approach: PostgreSQL dblink_send_query dispatches asynchronous SQL aggregates on separate backend connections; pg_backend_pid supplies the worker PID.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires PostgreSQL, dblink setup and authenticated connections. PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION handles failures natively; this edition remains untested.

references.match: -- Cancel and disconnect owned worker connections
references.label: Failure cleanup

adaptations.constraint: A database script has a client/server boundary rather than a single executable’s positional argv and local files.
adaptations.approach: psql variables supply options and a comma-separated prompt supplies interactive values. pg_read_file reads on the server; psql redirects ordered CSV output to a client-side file.
adaptations.tradeoff: Server input needs file-read privileges. The documented interface differs from line-at-a-time stdin and uses relational ordinals instead of pointers.

languages.name: Oberon-2
languages.runtime: Oxford Oberon-2 OBC 3 + POSIX C toolchain
languages.idioms: Modules, typed record pointers, VAR parameters, explicit error checks, LONGREAL quadrature.
languages.multiprocessing: Bounded fork/pipe batches through the supplied checked POSIX adapter.
languages.memory: Typed pointer owns a sample record; SYSTEM.ADR/GET and byte offsets traverse it without intervening allocations.
languages.strings: VAR-based in-place whitespace trimming, CHAR scanning, NUL-terminated CLI strings, checked numeric conversion.

adaptations.constraint: The core Oberon-2 language does not supply the POSIX/stdio services required by this executable.
adaptations.approach: Bessel.Mod imports the supplied C adapter for checked fork, pipes, complete transfers, waiting and file I/O. Scheduling, LONGREAL quadrature and address traversal stay in Oberon.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Oxford OBC, a C toolchain and POSIX. The adapter contains no Bessel kernel; input lines are bounded to 4095 bytes.

adaptations.constraint: This Oberon-2 implementation uses explicit status checks rather than catchable exception unwinding.
adaptations.approach: The adapter returns checked statuses; Fail emits a diagnostic, calls Cleanup, and HALTs with status 1.
adaptations.tradeoff: Failure paths must call the cleanup procedure explicitly; the adapter tracks owned streams, descriptors and child PIDs.

languages.name: RPG
languages.runtime: IBM i 7.5, ILE RPG + Db2 SQL + QC2LE; see rpg_setup.txt
languages.idioms: Fully free RPG, MONITOR/ON-ERROR, prototyped calls, embedded SQL, native job messages.
languages.multiprocessing: SBMJOB creates bounded IBM i batch jobs; dedicated queue must permit concurrent execution.
languages.memory: POINTER, %ADDR, BASED aliases, by-reference parameters, and byte-wise pointer advancement by %SIZE.
languages.strings: %TRIM, %CHECK, %SUBST, %SCANRPL, %CHAR, concatenation and CCSID-aware IFS services.
languages.integration_required: Requires an IBM i compiler, dedicated library, Db2 services and a configured batch queue; see rpg_setup.txt.

adaptations.objective: Real OS workers and result exchange
adaptations.constraint: IBM i uses submitted jobs and job queues rather than this project’s POSIX fork/pipe interface.
adaptations.approach: SBMJOB starts numeric batch jobs; Db2 WORK_ITEMS rows carry input, results and state. Bounded batches poll for completion and workers record getpid().
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires IBM i, configured queue/subsystem concurrency and database setup. Timeout is 600 seconds; failed rows remain and submitted jobs may finish after parent failure.

adaptations.constraint: The IBM i CALL/5250 interface differs from Unix argv, stdin and stderr.
adaptations.approach: Use padded CALL parameters, DSPLY input, Db2 IFS services and MONITOR/ON-ERROR. CheckSql translates SQL status into escape messages through Die.
adaptations.tradeoff: Paths are limited to 32 characters and interactive input needs a 5250 job. Errors use native job messages; compilation and execution remain untested.

languages.name: Bash
languages.runtime: Bash 4.3+ with awk and POSIX utilities
languages.idioms: Arrays, nameref, parameter expansion, background jobs, wait, traps, quoted paths, exec.
languages.multiprocessing: Background Bash workers exec awk; BASHPID remains the OS PID performing the numerical calculation.
languages.memory: Bash namerefs modify caller variables; character substring offsets are used honestly, with no raw pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: Whitespace parameter expansion, substring offsets, regex validation and printf.

adaptations.constraint: Bash arithmetic is integer-only and supplies no floating-point trigonometric kernel.
adaptations.approach: Each background worker execs the embedded awk quadrature. BASHPID is passed before exec, which preserves the PID of the process doing the math.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires awk. This edition explicitly delegates its numerical kernel; it is not an entirely Bash implementation.

adaptations.constraint: Shell exit statuses and traps provide no structured try/catch/finally scope.
adaptations.approach: Check commands and wait results, route fatal errors through fail, and use an EXIT trap to kill/reap outstanding workers and remove private row files.
adaptations.tradeoff: Every fallible operation needs an explicit check; cleanup uses tracked PIDs and temporary storage.

languages.name: Lingua::Romana::Perligata
languages.idioms: Latin-root vocabulary, inflected nouns and verbs, Roman numerals, sic/cis blocks, native evolute/scribe/claude I/O, adnota and ecce comments; separately browsable Perl compatibility module.
languages.multiprocessing: Latin scheduling loop uses registered Perl fork calls, bounded PID batches, checked waitpid and private per-observation files with parent-owned cleanup.
languages.memory: Latin ad creates a scalar reference for in-place trim; agtorem supplies a code reference to the exception boundary. Perl references retain their owners. No raw pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: Latin excerpementum (substr), serementum (concatenation), chr punctuation and a regex validation bridge; raw reads preserve decimal input instead of converting Roman numerals.

adaptations.constraint: Perligata 0.605 perlege converts Roman numerals, and its regex syntax is unimplemented.
adaptations.approach: BesselPerligata.pm exports accip for unchanged line reads and prob for complete finite-decimal validation. A line containing I stays invalid instead of becoming 1.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires the disclosed Perl compatibility module. Native Latin file opening, writing and closing remain in the main listing.

adaptations.constraint: The restricted Latin syntax needs access to checked Perl OS services and an exception boundary.
adaptations.approach: gign registers forked children, collig checks waitpid, and teg wraps the Latin action in eval and parent-owned cleanup. Private per-observation files carry ordered rows.
adaptations.tradeoff: The adapter handles OS/error mechanics; the Latin listing retains quadrature and scheduling. The helper is included in validation hashes.

languages.name: PostScript
languages.runtime: 64-bit Ghostscript on Linux; %pipe% and /proc access required
languages.idioms: Operand stacks, dictionaries, procedures, stopped error handling, and integer fixed-point arithmetic with 52 fractional bits.
languages.multiprocessing: PostScript schedules bounded batches of separate Ghostscript interpreters through %pipe%; Linux /proc supplies real PIDs.
languages.memory: Arrays and strings are reference objects; getinterval shares a bounded view. Input slices are copied before the line buffer is reused. No raw pointer arithmetic.
languages.strings: ASCII trimming, decimal/e-notation scanning, integer decimal formatting, shell argument quoting, and ordered CSV serialization.

adaptations.constraint: Ghostscript native real arithmetic has insufficient precision for the existing tolerance.
adaptations.approach: Implement decimal parsing, 52-bit fractional fixed-point multiplication, range-reduced trigonometry, accumulation and formatting entirely in PostScript using 64-bit integers.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires a 64-bit integer Ghostscript build and more arithmetic code. The tolerance and 16,384-sample quadrature are preserved; no foreign numerical helper is used.

adaptations.constraint: Portable PostScript does not specify the Linux process-launch and PID facilities used here.
adaptations.approach: Ghostscript %pipe% launches child interpreters and /proc supplies real PIDs. The internal POSIX shell only execs the interpreter; scheduling and result checks are PostScript.
adaptations.tradeoff: Requires Linux /proc and permitted %pipe% access. -dNOSAFER does not override OS restrictions such as AppArmor.

adaptations.constraint: Native stop/stopped catches control transfer but does not restore operand and dictionary stacks automatically.
adaptations.approach: Record stack depths before parsing, restore them after a rejected token, and continue input. The top-level stopped boundary reports fatal errors and closes tracked files/pipes.
adaptations.tradeoff: Error handling is native; explicit stack restoration and resource cleanup are still required.

memory_policy: Explicit raw-pointer examples are small, bounds-limited demonstrations over storage whose owner stays alive. In safe or relational languages, document the absence of raw-pointer arithmetic and show native references, views or ordinal access instead. No shared native helper performs the mathematics.

postscript_design.choice: This edition keeps the existing 1e-10 absolute tolerance and implements all numerical work in PostScript, without a numerical helper or precision exception.
postscript_design.reason: Ghostscript reals are single precision even in a 64-bit build. The nearest binary32 representation of J0(1) already differs by about 7.74e-9.
postscript_design.arithmetic: Signed 64-bit integers store fixed-point values with 52 fractional bits. Split 26-bit products, integer range reduction, Taylor cosine, decimal parsing/formatting and quotient/remainder summation preserve precision without native real arithmetic.
postscript_design.method: The same 16,384 midpoint samples are evaluated. Software arithmetic changes the representation, not the integral, domain, sample count or tolerance.
postscript_design.processes: All scheduling is PostScript. Ghostscript %pipe% uses the POSIX shell only to exec the same interpreter via /proc/PID/exe; each child reads its own real PID from /proc/self/stat. No helper source in another language.
postscript_design.setup: Run from the project directory with 64-bit Ghostscript, Linux /proc and -dNOSAFER for OS access. OS policies such as a printer-only AppArmor profile can still deny subprocesses or files. A different working directory requires -sBesselSource=/absolute/path/bessel.ps before --.
postscript_design.input_limit: Input lines are bounded to 4096 bytes; longer lines fail with a readable diagnostic. Decimal input is parsed with less than 2^-52 + 1e-18 absolute truncation error.
